metadata.title: Automorphism group of split Cartan modular curves

nodes.name: Split Cartan modular curve $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$
nodes.statement: For a prime integer $p$, let $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ be the modular curve defined over $\Q$ attached to the congruence subgroup of level $p$ $$ \Gamma_{\operatorname{split}}(p)=\left\{ \left (\begin{array}{cc}a &b\\c& d\end{array}\right)\in\SL_2(\Z)\colon b\equiv c\equiv 0 \text{ or }a\equiv d\equiv 0\right\}\,. $$
nodes.statement_short: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is the modular curve over $\Q$ attached to the level-$p$ split Cartan congruence subgroup $\Gamma_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$.
differentia: attached to the congruence subgroup of level $p$ $$ \Gamma_{\operatorname{split}}(p)=\left\{ \left (\begin{array}{cc}a &b\\c& d\end{array}\right)\in\SL_2(\Z)\colon b\equiv c\equiv 0 \text{ or }a\equiv d\equiv 0\right\}\,. $$
nodes.origin_citation: classical definition of the split Cartan modular curve

nodes.name: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)\simeq X_0^+(p^2)$ over $\Q$
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is isomorphic over $\Q$ to the modular curve $X_0^+(p^2):=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$, where $w_{p^2}$ stands for the Fricke involution. The genus of this curve is positive when $p\geq 11$ and, in this case, it is at least $2$.
nodes.statement_short: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is $\Q$-isomorphic to $X_0^+(p^2)=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$, whose genus is $\geq 2$ for $p\geq 11$.
conclusions: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is isomorphic over $\Q$ to the modular curve $X_0^+(p^2):=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$
The genus of this curve is positive when $p\geq 11$ and, in this case, it is at least $2$

nodes.name: Prior determination of $\Aut(X_0(N))$ (Kenku-Momose, Elkies)
nodes.statement: The automorphism group of the modular curve $X_0(N)$ was determined, except for $N=63$, by Kenku and Momose in \cite{KM} and was completed by Elkies in \cite{elkies}.

nodes.name: Prior determination of $\Aut(X_0^+(p))$ (Baker-Hasegawa)
nodes.statement: Later, the automorphism group of the modular curve $X_0^+(p)=X_0(p)/w_p$ was determined by Baker and Hasegawa in \cite{BH}.

nodes.name: Automorphism group of the split Cartan modular curve $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$
nodes.statement: Assume that the genus of $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is positive. Then, $$\Aut(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))=\Aut_{\Q}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))\simeq\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \{1\} & \text{if $p>11$,}\\[5 pt] (\Z/2\Z)^2 & \text{if $p=11$.}\end{array}\right. $$
nodes.statement_short: For positive genus, $\Aut(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))$ is all defined over $\Q$ and is trivial for $p>11$, and $(\Z/2\Z)^2$ for $p=11$.
assumptions: Assume that the genus of $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is positive.
conclusions: $$\Aut(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))=\Aut_{\Q}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))\simeq\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \{1\} & \text{if $p>11$,}\\[5 pt] (\Z/2\Z)^2 & \text{if $p=11$.}\end{array}\right. $$

nodes.name: Character twist $f_\chi$ of a newform
nodes.statement: for a normalized newform $f=\sum_{n\geq 1} a_n q^n\in S_2(\Gamma_1(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$ of conductor $N'$, the function $$f_\chi:=\sum_{n\geq 1} \chi(n)a_n q^n$$

nodes.name: Twist $f_\chi$ is a cusp form of level $\operatorname{lcm}(N,N'^2)$
nodes.statement: We recall that, for a normalized newform $f=\sum_{n\geq 1} a_n q^n\in S_2(\Gamma_1(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$ of conductor $N'$, the function $$f_\chi:=\sum_{n\geq 1} \chi(n)a_n q^n$$ is a cusp form in $S_2(\Gamma_1(\operatorname{lcm} (N, {N'}^2))$ (cf. Proposition 3.1 de \cite{Atkin}).
nodes.statement_short: Twisting a weight-2 newform of level $N$ by a character of conductor $N'$ gives a cusp form of level $\operatorname{lcm}(N,N'^2)$.
assumptions: a normalized newform $f=\sum_{n\geq 1} a_n q^n\in S_2(\Gamma_1(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$
conclusions: the function $$f_\chi:=\sum_{n\geq 1} \chi(n)a_n q^n$$ is a cusp form in $S_2(\Gamma_1(\operatorname{lcm} (N, {N'}^2))$

nodes.name: Twisted newform $f\otimes\chi$
nodes.statement: Let $f\otimes \chi$ denote the unique normalized newform with $q$-expansion $\sum_{n\geq 1} b_n q^n$ that satisfies $b_{\ell}=\chi(\ell) a_{\ell}$ for all primes $\ell\nmid N\cdot N'$.
differentia: with $q$-expansion $\sum_{n\geq 1} b_n q^n$ that satisfies $b_{\ell}=\chi(\ell) a_{\ell}$ for all primes $\ell\nmid N\cdot N'$

nodes.name: Level comparison between $f\otimes\chi$ and $f_\chi$
nodes.statement: If $f\otimes \chi$ is a newform of level $M$ and $f_\chi$ has level $M'$, then $M|M'$. Moreover, if $M=M'$, then $f_\chi=f\otimes\chi$.
conclusions: if $M=M'$, then $f_\chi=f\otimes\chi$

nodes.name: $\New_N$, the set of normalized newforms of level $N$
nodes.statement: Let $\New_N$ denote the set of normalized newforms in $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$.

nodes.name: Fricke eigenvalue $\varepsilon(f)$
nodes.statement: For $f\in\New_N$, $\varepsilon(f)$ denotes the eigenvalue of $f$ under the action of the Fricke involution $w_N$
differentia: under the action of the Fricke involution $w_N$

nodes.name: $\New_N^+$, newforms with Fricke eigenvalue $1$
nodes.statement: set $\New_N^+=\{f\in \New_N\colon \varepsilon(f)=1\}$

nodes.name: $S_2(f)$, the space spanned by $f$ and its Galois conjugates
nodes.statement: For a cusp form $f=\sum_n b_n q^n \in S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$ such that $\Q(\{b_n\})$ is a number field, $S_2(f)$ denotes the $\C$-vector space of cusp forms spanned by $f$ and its Galois conjugates.
differentia: spanned by $f$ and its Galois conjugates

nodes.name: Abelian variety $A_f$ attached to $f$ by Shimura
nodes.statement: In the particular case that $f\in\New_N$, $A_f$ stands for the abelian variety attached to $f$ by Shimura.

nodes.name: Properties of $A_f$: quotient of $J_0(N)$ and totally real endomorphism algebra
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $A_f$ is a quotient of $J_0(N):=\Jac (X_0(N))$ defined over $\Q$ and the pull-back of $\Omega^1_{A_f/\Q}$ is the $\Q$-vector subspace of elements in $S_2(f) dq/q$ with rational $q$-expansion, i.e. $S_2(f) dq/q\cap\Q[[q]]$. Moreover, the endomorphism algebra $\End_\Q(A_f)\otimes \Q$ is a totally real number field.
nodes.statement_short: $A_f$ is a $\Q$-quotient of $J_0(N)$ with differentials cut out by $S_2(f)dq/q$, and $\End_\Q(A_f)\otimes\Q$ is totally real.
conclusions: $A_f$ is a quotient of $J_0(N):=\Jac (X_0(N))$ defined over $\Q$
the pull-back of $\Omega^1_{A_f/\Q}$ is the $\Q$-vector subspace of elements in $S_2(f) dq/q$ with rational $q$-expansion, i.e. $S_2(f) dq/q\cap\Q[[q]]$
the endomorphism algebra $\End_\Q(A_f)\otimes \Q$ is a totally real number field

nodes.name: Standing assumption $p\geq 11$
nodes.statement: From now on, we assume $p\geq 11$

nodes.name: Quadratic character $\chi$ of conductor $p$ and the field $K=\Q(\sqrt{p^*})$
nodes.statement: $\chi$ denotes the quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor $p$, i.e. the Dirichlet character attached to the quadratic number field $K=\Q(\sqrt{p^*})$, where $p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$.
nodes.genus: the quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor $p$
differentia: attached to the quadratic number field $K=\Q(\sqrt{p^*})$, where $p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$

nodes.name: The twist map $f\mapsto f\otimes\chi$ permutes $\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p$
nodes.statement: The map $f\mapsto f\otimes \chi$ is a permutation of the set $\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p$. Under this bijection, there is a unique newform $f$, up to Galois conjugation, such that $f=f\otimes \chi$ when $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting by $\chi$ permutes $\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p$, with a unique fixed newform (up to conjugation) exactly when $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$.
assumptions: $\chi$ denotes the quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor $p$
conclusions: The map $f\mapsto f\otimes \chi$ is a permutation of the set $\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p$.
there is a unique newform $f$, up to Galois conjugation, such that $f=f\otimes \chi$ when $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$

nodes.name: Proof that $f\mapsto f\otimes\chi$ permutes $\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p$
nodes.statement: Since $f_\chi\in S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))$ for $f\in\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p$ (cf. Theorem 3.1 of \cite{Atkin}), the level of $f\otimes\chi$ divides $p^2$ and, thus, the map is well defined. The injectivity follows from the fact that $(f\otimes\chi)\otimes\chi=f$. The condition $f=f\otimes\chi$ amounts to saying that $f$ has complex multiplication (CM) by the imaginary quadratic field $K$ attached to $\chi$, i.e. $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and, moreover, $f$ is obtained from a Hecke character $\psi$ whose conductor is the ideal of $K$ of norm $p$, which implies $f\in\New_{p^2}$. Since $f$ has trivial Nebentypus, the Hecke character $\psi$ is unique up to Galois conjugation.
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness from level bounds on twists, injectivity from $(f\otimes\chi)\otimes\chi=f$, and the fixed point identified via CM by $K$.

nodes.name: The twist map is well defined
nodes.statement: Since $f_\chi\in S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))$ for $f\in\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p$ (cf. Theorem 3.1 of \cite{Atkin}), the level of $f\otimes\chi$ divides $p^2$ and, thus, the map is well defined.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the level of $f\otimes\chi$ by $p^2$ to see the map lands in the same set.

nodes.name: Injectivity of the twist map
nodes.statement: The injectivity follows from the fact that $(f\otimes\chi)\otimes\chi=f$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity from the involutivity of twisting by the quadratic character $\chi$.

nodes.name: Identification of the fixed newform via CM
nodes.statement: The condition $f=f\otimes\chi$ amounts to saying that $f$ has complex multiplication (CM) by the imaginary quadratic field $K$ attached to $\chi$, i.e. $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and, moreover, $f$ is obtained from a Hecke character $\psi$ whose conductor is the ideal of $K$ of norm $p$, which implies $f\in\New_{p^2}$. Since $f$ has trivial Nebentypus, the Hecke character $\psi$ is unique up to Galois conjugation.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed points of the twist correspond to CM forms from a Hecke character of $K$, unique up to conjugation.

nodes.name: Twisting need not preserve the Fricke eigenvalue
nodes.statement: The above map does not preserve the eigenvalue of the corresponding Fricke involution, i.e. it may be that $\varepsilon(f)$ and $\varepsilon(f\otimes \chi)$ are different.

nodes.name: Inner twists of newforms of level $p$ or $p^2$
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \New_{p^2}\cup \New_p$ without CM. If $f$ has an inner twist $\chi'\neq 1$, i.e. $f\otimes \chi'={}^{\sigma} f$ for some $\sigma\in G_\Q:=\Gal (\overline{\Q}/\Q)$, then $\chi'=\chi$ because $\chi'$ must be a quadratic character of conductor dividing $p^2$. In such a case, $\End (A_f)\otimes\Q=\End_K(A_f)\otimes \Q$ is a non commutative algebra. Otherwise, $\End (A_f)\otimes\Q=\End_\Q(A_f)\otimes \Q$ is a totally real umber field.
nodes.statement_short: For non-CM $f$ the only possible inner twist is $\chi$; its presence makes $\End(A_f)\otimes\Q$ noncommutative, otherwise totally real.

nodes.name: CM newforms of level $p^2$: dimension, splitting field, and Fricke sign
nodes.statement: If $f\in\New_{p^2}$ has CM, then the dimension of $A_f$ is the class number of $K$, $A_f$ has all its endomorphisms defined over the Hilbert class field of $K$ and $\End_K(A_f)\otimes\Q$ is the CM field $\End_\Q(A_f)\otimes K$ which only contains the roots of the unity $\pm 1$ (cf. Theorem 1.2 of of \cite{gola011} and part (3) in Proposition 3.2 of \cite{Yang2}). Moreover, $f\in\New_{p^2}^+$ if, and only if, $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ (cf. Corollary 6.3 of \cite{Yang1}).
nodes.statement_short: For CM $f$ of level $p^2$: $\dim A_f$ is the class number of $K$, endomorphisms are defined over the Hilbert class field, and $\varepsilon(f)=1$ iff $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$.
nodes.origin_citation: cf. Theorem 1.2 of [gola011], Proposition 3.2(3) of [Yang2], Corollary 6.3 of [Yang1]

nodes.name: Isogeny criterion for $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$
nodes.statement: For two distinct $f_1, f_2\in(\New_{p^2}\cup\New_p)/G_\Q$, the abelian varieties $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$ are nonisogenous over $\Q$ and are isogenous if, and only if, $f_1\otimes \chi={}^{\sigma} f_2$ for some $\sigma\in G_\Q$ (see Proposition 4.2 of \cite{goji}) and, in this particular case, there is an isogeny defined over $K$.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct Galois classes give $\Q$-nonisogenous $A_f$; they become isogenous over $K$ exactly when the classes are twists by $\chi$.

nodes.name: $\Q$-splitting of $J_0^+(p^2)$
nodes.statement: The abelian variety $J_0^+(p^2):=\Jac (X_0^+(p^2))$ splits over $\Q$ as the product $(J_0(p^2)^{\new})^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}\times J_0(p)$. More precisely, \begin{equation} J_0^+(p^2)\stackrel{\Q}\sim \prod_{f\in(\New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p)/G_{\Q}} A_f\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $J_0^+(p^2)$ is $\Q$-isogenous to the product of the $A_f$ over Galois classes in $\New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p$.
conclusions: The abelian variety $J_0^+(p^2):=\Jac (X_0^+(p^2))$ splits over $\Q$ as the product $(J_0(p^2)^{\new})^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}\times J_0(p)$
J_0^+(p^2)\stackrel{\Q}\sim \prod_{f\in(\New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p)/G_{\Q}} A_f\,.

nodes.name: Oldform eigenvectors of $w_{p^2}$ coming from $\New_p$
nodes.statement: Each $f\in \New_p$ provides a vector subspace of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\operatorname{old}}$ of dimension $2$ genera\-ted by $f(q)$ and $f(q^p)$. The normalized cusp forms $f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ and $f(q)-p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ are eigenforms for all Hecke operators $T_m$ with $p\nmid m$ and the Fricke involution $w_{p^2}$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Each level-$p$ newform yields a 2-dimensional oldspace whose combinations $f(q)\pm p\varepsilon(f)f(q^p)$ are $w_{p^2}$-eigenforms of eigenvalue $\pm 1$.
conclusions: a vector subspace of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\operatorname{old}}$ of dimension $2$ genera\-ted by $f(q)$ and $f(q^p)$

The normalized cusp forms $f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ and $f(q)-p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ are eigenforms for all Hecke operators $T_m$ with $p\nmid m$ and the Fricke involution $w_{p^2}$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively
nodes.origin_citation: standard oldform theory, recalled without proof

nodes.name: Decomposition of $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}$
nodes.statement: The splitting of $J_0^+(p^2)$ over $\Q$ provides the following decomposition for its vector space of regular differentials \begin{equation} \Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}=\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\New_{p^2}^+/G_\Q}S_2(f(q))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\bigoplus\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\New_{p}/G_\Q} S_2(f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The regular differentials of $J_0^+(p^2)$ decompose into the $S_2(f(q))$ for $f\in\New_{p^2}^+$ plus the $S_2(f(q)+p\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))$ for $f\in\New_p$.

nodes.name: Genera $g^+$ and $g_0$
nodes.statement: Let $g^+$ and $g_0$ be the genus of the curves $ X_0^+(p^2)$ and $X_0(p)$, respectively.

nodes.name: Table of genus values $g^+$ and $g_0$ by $p \bmod 12$
nodes.statement: From the genus formula for these curves, one obtains the following values $$ \begin{array}{c|c|c|} p & g^+ &g_0\\ \hline\hline p\equiv 1 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{\frac{(p-1)(p-7)}{24}} & \displaystyle{\frac{p-13}{12}}\\[6 pt] p\equiv 5 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{ \frac{(p-3)(p-5)}{24} } & \displaystyle{\frac{p-5}{12} }\\[6 pt] p\equiv 7 \pmod{12} & \displaystyle{ \frac{(p-1)(p-7)}{24} }&\displaystyle{\frac{p-7}{12}} \\[6 pt] p\equiv 11 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{ \frac{(p-3)(p-5)}{24} } & \displaystyle{\frac{p+1}{12}}\\\hline \end{array} $$
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form genus values for $X_0^+(p^2)$ and $X_0(p)$ in each residue class of $p$ modulo $12$.

nodes.name: Hyperelliptic case: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ hyperelliptic iff $p=11$
nodes.statement: Assume $p\geq 11 $. Then, $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is hyperelliptic if, and only if, $p=11$. Moreover, one has $$\Aut (X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))=\Aut_{\Q}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))\simeq (\Z/2\Z)^2\,. $$
nodes.statement_short: For $p\geq 11$, $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is hyperelliptic only for $p=11$, where its full automorphism group is $(\Z/2\Z)^2$ and defined over $\Q$.
conclusions: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is hyperelliptic if, and only if, $p=11$
$$\Aut (X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))=\Aut_{\Q}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))\simeq (\Z/2\Z)^2\,. $$

nodes.name: Lemma 2.5 of [BGGP]: normalized basis and hyperelliptic model
nodes.statement: Lemma 2.5 of \cite{BGGP} states that there is a basis $f_1,\cdots, f_{g^+}$ of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ with rational $q$-expansions satisfying \begin{equation} f_i(q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cr} q^i+ O(q^i)&\text{ if the cusp $\infty$ is not a Weierstrass point of $X_0^+ (p^2)$,}\\q^{2 i-1}+ O(q^{2i-1})& \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right. \end{equation} Moreover, for any such a basis, the functions on $X_0 ^+(p^2)$ defined by $$ x=\frac{f_{g^+}}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,\quad y=\frac{ q dx/dq}{f_{g^+-1}}\,, $$ satisfy $y^2=P(x)$ for a unique squarefree polynomial $P(X)\in\Q[X]$ which has degree $2g^++1$ or $2g^++2$ depending on whether $\infty$ is a Weierstrass point or not.
nodes.statement_short: A hyperelliptic $X_0^+(p^2)$ admits a $q$-normalized rational basis of cusp forms, from which $x,y$ give the unique squarefree hyperelliptic model $y^2=P(x)$.
assumptions: there is a basis $f_1,\cdots, f_{g^+}$ of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ with rational $q$-expansions
conclusions: the functions on $X_0 ^+(p^2)$ defined by $$ x=\frac{f_{g^+}}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,\quad y=\frac{ q dx/dq}{f_{g^+-1}}\,, $$ satisfy $y^2=P(x)$ for a unique squarefree polynomial $P(X)\in\Q[X]$
which has degree $2g^++1$ or $2g^++2$ depending on whether $\infty$ is a Weierstrass point or not

nodes.name: Normalized $q$-expansion condition on the basis $f_i$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} f_i(q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cr} q^i+ O(q^i)&\text{ if the cusp $\infty$ is not a Weierstrass point of $X_0^+ (p^2)$,}\\q^{2 i-1}+ O(q^{2i-1})& \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Leading-order normalization of the basis forms, differing according to whether $\infty$ is a Weierstrass point.

nodes.name: Hyperelliptic equation of $X_0^+(11^2)$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation}y^2= x^6 -7 x^4+11 x^2+11\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit genus-2 model of $X_0^+(11^2)$ obtained from $q$-expansions.

nodes.name: Proof of the hyperelliptic classification and $\Aut(X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))$
nodes.statement: Assume $X_0^+(p^2)$ is hyperelliptic. By applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP}, we obtain $g^+\leq 10$, which implies $p\leq 19$. We have $g^+=2$ if, and only if, $p=11$ and, thus, the curve $X_0^+(11^2)$ is hyperelliptic. For $p>11$, on has $g^+>2$ and, moreover, $p>13$ because $X_0^+(13^2)$ is a plane quartic (cf. \cite{Baran}). Lemma 2.5 of \cite{BGGP} states that there is a basis $f_1,\cdots, f_{g^+}$ of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ with rational $q$-expansions satisfying \begin{equation} f_i(q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cr} q^i+ O(q^i)&\text{ if the cusp $\infty$ is not a Weierstrass point of $X_0^+ (p^2)$,}\\q^{2 i-1}+ O(q^{2i-1})& \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right. \end{equation} Moreover, for any such a basis, the functions on $X_0 ^+(p^2)$ defined by $$ x=\frac{f_{g^+}}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,\quad y=\frac{ q dx/dq}{f_{g^+-1}}\,, $$ satisfy $y^2=P(x)$ for a unique squarefree polynomial $P(X)\in\Q[X]$ which has degree $2g^++1$ or $2g^++2$ depending on whether $\infty$ is a Weierstrass point or not. The first part of the statement follows from the fact that, for $p=17$ and $p=19$, the vector space $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ does not have any bases as in (\ref{congq}). Now, we consider $p=11$. In this case, $|\New_{11^2}|=|\New_{11}|=1$. Let $f_1\in\New_{11^2}^+$ and let $f_2\in\New_{11}$. The newform $f_1$ is the one attached to the elliptic curve $E_1/\Q$ of conductor $11^2$ with CM by $\Z[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]$, and $f_2$ is the newform attached to an elliptic curve $E_2/\Q$ of conductor $11$ without CM. Since $\varepsilon(f_2)=-1$, the cusp forms $f_1(q)$ and $h(q)=f_2(q)-11 f_2(q^{11})$ are a basis of $S_2(\Gamma_0(11^2))^{\langle w_{11^2}\rangle}$. Take the following functions on $X_0^+(11^2)$ $$ x=\frac{h}{f_1}=1 - 2 q + 2 q^3 - 2 q^5 + O(q^5)\,,\quad y=-2 \frac{q\,dx/q}{f_1}=4 - 8 q^2 + 8 q^3 + 24 q^4 - 32 q^5+ O(q^5)\,. $$ Using $q$-expansions, we get the following equation for $X_0^+(11^2)$: \begin{equation}y^2= x^6 -7 x^4+11 x^2+11\,. \end{equation}The maps $(x,y)\mapsto (\pm x,\pm y) $ provide a subgroup of $\Aut_\Q(X_0^+(11^2))$ isomorphic to $(\Z/2\Z)^2$. Since $\Aut_{\overline\Q}(X_0^+(11^2))$ is a finite subgroup of $\End(E_1)\times \End(E_2)\simeq \Z[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]\times\Z$, we have that it must be a subgroup of $(\Z/2\Z)^2$, which proves the second part of the statement.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the genus to reduce to $p\leq 19$, rule out $p=17,19$ by the nonexistence of a normalized basis, then compute the genus-2 model for $p=11$ and bound $\Aut$ inside $\End(E_1)\times\End(E_2)$.

nodes.name: Genus bound forces $p\leq 19$
nodes.statement: Assume $X_0^+(p^2)$ is hyperelliptic. By applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP}, we obtain $g^+\leq 10$, which implies $p\leq 19$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the [BGGP] point-count bound to get $g^+\leq 10$, hence $p\leq 19$.

nodes.name: Small primes: $p=11$ works, $p=13$ excluded
nodes.statement: We have $g^+=2$ if, and only if, $p=11$ and, thus, the curve $X_0^+(11^2)$ is hyperelliptic. For $p>11$, on has $g^+>2$ and, moreover, $p>13$ because $X_0^+(13^2)$ is a plane quartic (cf. \cite{Baran}).
nodes.statement_short: Identify $g^+=2$ exactly for $p=11$ and exclude $p=13$ since $X_0^+(13^2)$ is a plane quartic.

nodes.name: Rule out $p=17,19$ by absence of a normalized basis
nodes.statement: The first part of the statement follows from the fact that, for $p=17$ and $p=19$, the vector space $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ does not have any bases as in (\ref{congq}).
nodes.statement_short: Apply the [BGGP] basis criterion to exclude $p=17,19$, finishing the first assertion.

nodes.name: Explicit model for $p=11$ from $q$-expansions
nodes.statement: Now, we consider $p=11$. In this case, $|\New_{11^2}|=|\New_{11}|=1$. Let $f_1\in\New_{11^2}^+$ and let $f_2\in\New_{11}$. nodes.name: A nontrivial automorphism does not send $\infty$ to a cusp

nodes.name: Proof that $u(\infty)$ is not a cusp
nodes.statement: The modular curve $X_0(p^2)$ has $p+1$ cusps. Only the cusps $\infty$ and $0$ are defined over $\Q$. The remaining cusps $1/p,\cdots, (p-1)/p$ are defined over the $p$-th cyclotomic field $\Q(\zeta_p)$. The Galois group $\Gal(\Q(\zeta_p)/\Q)$ acts transitively on this set, and the cusp $w_{p^2}(i/p)=(p-i)/p$ is the complex conjugate of the cusp $i/p$ (cf. \cite{Ogg}). Hence, among the $(p+1)/2$ cusps of $X_0^+(p^2)$ the cusp $\infty$ is the only one defined over the quadratic field $K$. Let $u$ be an automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$ such that $u(\infty)$ is a cusp. By Lemma \ref{defi}, $u(\infty)$ is defined over $K$ and, thus, $u(\infty)=\infty$. Let $\Q [[q]]$ be the completion of the local ring $\cO_{X_0^+(p^2),\infty}$ with respect to the local parameter $q$. If $u(\infty)$ is the cusp $\infty$, then $u^*(q)=\zeta_m q+\sum_{n>1} c_i q^i$, where $\zeta_m$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity and, thus, $u$ is defined over $\Q (\zeta_m)$. Since the unique roots of unity in $K$ are $\pm 1$, it follows that $u$ is defined over $\Q$. Now, we will prove that, if $u\in\Aut_\Q(X_0^+(p^2))$ is nontrivial, then $u(\infty)\neq \infty$. For the hyperelliptic case $p=11$, the cusp $\infty$ has $(1,4)$ as $(x,y)$ coordinates in the equation given in (\ref{eq}). Hence, $\infty$ is not a fixed point for any of the three nontrivial involutions of $X_{0}^+(11^2)$. Let $p>11$. Since $X_0^+(p^2)$ is nonhyperelliptic and, by Lemma \ref{overQ}, $u$ is an involution, we can exclude the case where all eigenvalues of $u$ acting on $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}$ are equal to $-1$ and, thus, $u$ must have eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ acting on this vector space. The vector space of cusp forms $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)} {q}/{dq}$ has a basis of normalized eigenforms (see (\ref{diferencial})). Since $u$ is defined over $\Q$, $u$ commutes with the Hecke operators and, thus, there are two normalized eigenforms such that their corresponding regular differentials $\omega_1=(1+\sum_{n>1} a_n q^n)dq$ and $\omega_2=(1+\sum_{n>1} b_n q^n)dq$ satisfy $u^*(\omega_1)=\omega_1$ and $u^*(\omega_2)=-\omega_2$. Hence, $u$ sends $\omega_1+\omega_2$, which does vanish at $\infty$, to $\omega_1-\omega_2$, which vanishes at $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: $\infty$ is the only cusp of $X_0^+(p^2)$ rational over $K$, so $u(\infty)=\infty$ forces $u$ over $\Q$, which is impossible by the $p=11$ model and by an eigenform vanishing argument for $p>11$.

nodes.name: The gonality lemma adapts Lemma 3.3 of [BH]
nodes.statement: The following lemma is an adapted version of Lemma 3.3 of \cite{BH} to our context, restricted to the prime $2$.

nodes.name: Gonality bound and bound on fixed points of a nontrivial automorphism
nodes.statement: Assume that $u\in\Aut (X_0^+(p^2))$ is nontrivial. For any noncuspidal point $S\in X_0^+(p^2)({\C})$, the divisor $$D_S:=(u T_2 -T_2 u^\nu)\left(\infty-S\right)\,,$$ where $T_2$ denotes de Hecke operator viewed as a correspondence of the curve $X_0^+(p^2)$, is nonzero but linearly equivalent to zero. nodes.name: Only $p\in\{17,19,23,29,31\}$ can admit a nontrivial automorphism
nodes.statement: If $X_0^+(p^2)$ has a nontrivial automorphism and $p>11$, then $p\in\{ 17,19,23,29,31\}$.

nodes.name: Proof that $p\leq 31$ and $p\neq 13$
nodes.statement: By applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP} for the prime $2$, we obtain that $$g^+ < X_0^+(p^2)(\F_4)+1 \,.$$ By Lemma \ref{gonality}, the $\F_4$-gonality of $X_0^+(p)\otimes \F_{4}$ is $\leq 6$ and, thus, $X_0^+(p)(\F_4)\leq 30$. Hence, $g^+\leq 30$, which implies $p\leq 31$. The algebra $\End(J_0^+(13^2))\otimes\Q $ is a totally real number field and, thus, it only contains the roots of unity $\pm 1$. Since $X_0^+(13^2)$ is nonhyperelliptic, $\Aut(X_0^+(13^2))$ is trivial and we can discard the case $p=13$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the [BGGP] point-count bound with the gonality bound to force $g^+\leq 30$ hence $p\leq 31$, then discard $p=13$ using its totally real endomorphism algebra.

nodes.name: Point-count bound at the prime $2$
nodes.statement: By applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP} for the prime $2$, we obtain that $$g^+ < X_0^+(p^2)(\F_4)+1 \,.$$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the [BGGP] bound to compare $g^+$ with the number of $\F_4$-points.

nodes.name: Gonality bound gives $p\leq 31$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{gonality}, the $\F_4$-gonality of $X_0^+(p)\otimes \F_{4}$ is $\leq 6$ and, thus, $X_0^+(p)(\F_4)\leq 30$. Hence, $g^+\leq 30$, which implies $p\leq 31$.
nodes.statement_short: Gonality $\leq 6$ caps $\F_4$-points at $30$, so $g^+\leq 30$ and $p\leq 31$.

nodes.name: Discard $p=13$
nodes.statement: The algebra $\End(J_0^+(13^2))\otimes\Q $ is a totally real number field and, thus, it only contains the roots of unity $\pm 1$. Since $X_0^+(13^2)$ is nonhyperelliptic, $\Aut(X_0^+(13^2))$ is trivial and we can discard the case $p=13$.
nodes.statement_short: Totally real endomorphism algebra plus nonhyperellipticity make $\Aut(X_0^+(13^2))$ trivial.

nodes.name: Every nontrivial automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$ has even order
nodes.statement: Every nontrivial automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$ has even order.
conclusions: Every nontrivial automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$ has even order.

nodes.name: Proof that nontrivial automorphisms have even order
nodes.statement: Assume that there is a nontrivial automorphism $u$ of $X_0^+(p^2)$ whose order $m$ is odd. Let $X_u$ be the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/ u$ and denote by $ g_u$ its genus. Next, we find a positive lower bound $t$ for $g_u$. The endomorphism algebra $\End_K(J_0^+(p^2))\otimes \Q$ is the product of some noncommutative algebras and some number fields $E_f=\End_K (A_f)\otimes\Q$ attached to the newforms $f$ lying in a certain subset $\cS$ of $ (\New_{p^2}^+\cup \New_p)/G_\Q$. The set $\cS$ is formed by newforms $f$ without CM such that $f\otimes \chi\notin \New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p$ ($E_f=\End_\Q(A_f)$ is a totally real number field) and by a newform $f$ with CM by $K$ if $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ ($E_f=\End_\Q(A_f)\otimes K$ is a CM field). For $f\in\cS$, the unique root of unities contained in $E_f$ are $\pm 1$. Since $m$ is odd, the automorphism $u$ must act on each $E_f$ as the identity and, thus, we have $$t:= \sum_{f\in \cS}\dim A_f\leq g_u\,.$$ An easy computation provides the following values for $t$: $$ \begin{array}{c|ccccc|} p& 17 &19 &23 & 29& 31\\\hline\hline g^+&7 & 9& 15& 26 & 30\\ t&5 & 5& 7& 15 & 12\\ \hline \end{array} $$ Applying Riemann-Hurwitz formula, $$\displaystyle{m\leq \frac{g^+-1}{g_u-1}\leq \frac{g^+-1}{t-1}}<3\,,$$which yields a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: an odd-order $u$ acts trivially on all number-field factors, forcing $g_u\geq t$, and Riemann-Hurwitz then gives $m<3$.

nodes.name: Assume odd order and set up the quotient curve
nodes.statement: Assume that there is a nontrivial automorphism $u$ of $X_0^+(p^2)$ whose order $m$ is odd. Let $X_u$ be the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/ u$ and denote by $ g_u$ its genus. Next, we find a positive lower bound $t$ for $g_u$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the contradiction hypothesis and the quotient curve of genus $g_u$.

nodes.name: Structure of $\End_K(J_0^+(p^2))\otimes\Q$ and the set $\cS$
nodes.statement: The endomorphism algebra $\End_K(J_0^+(p^2))\otimes \Q$ is the product of some noncommutative algebras and some number fields $E_f=\End_K (A_f)\otimes\Q$ attached to the newforms $f$ lying in a certain subset $\cS$ of $ (\New_{p^2}^+\cup \New_p)/G_\Q$. The set $\cS$ is formed by newforms $f$ without CM such that $f\otimes \chi\notin \New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p$ ($E_f=\End_\Q(A_f)$ is a totally real number field) and by a newform $f$ with CM by $K$ if $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ ($E_f=\End_\Q(A_f)\otimes K$ is a CM field).
nodes.statement_short: Describe the number-field factors of the $K$-endomorphism algebra and the indexing set $\cS$.

nodes.name: Lower bound $t\leq g_u$ and its values
nodes.statement: For $f\in\cS$, the unique root of unities contained in $E_f$ are $\pm 1$. Since $m$ is odd, the automorphism $u$ must act on each $E_f$ as the identity and, thus, we have $$t:= \sum_{f\in \cS}\dim A_f\leq g_u\,.$$ An easy computation provides the following values for $t$: $$ \begin{array}{c|ccccc|} p& 17 &19 &23 & 29& 31\\\hline\hline g^+&7 & 9& 15& 26 & 30\\ t&5 & 5& 7& 15 & 12\\ \hline \end{array} $$
nodes.statement_short: Odd order forces trivial action on each $E_f$, giving the lower bound $t\leq g_u$ with explicit values.

nodes.name: Riemann-Hurwitz contradiction
nodes.statement: Applying Riemann-Hurwitz formula, $$\displaystyle{m\leq \frac{g^+-1}{g_u-1}\leq \frac{g^+-1}{t-1}}<3\,,$$which yields a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Hurwitz forces $m<3$, contradicting that $m$ is odd and $>1$.

nodes.name: The counting function $N_\ell(n)$
nodes.statement: We write $$ N_{\ell}(n):=1+\ell^n-\sum_{i=1}^{2 g^+}\alpha_i^n\,, $$ where $\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_{2 g^+}$ are the roots of polynomial $$ \prod_{f\in \New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p}(x^2-a_{\ell}(f) x+\ell) $$ and $a_{\ell}(f)$ is the $\ell$-th Fourier coefficient of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: $N_\ell(n)$ is the Weil-type point count built from the roots of the characteristic polynomials of the Fourier coefficients $a_\ell(f)$.
differentia: $\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_{2 g^+}$ are the roots of polynomial $$ \prod_{f\in \New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p}(x^2-a_{\ell}(f) x+\ell) $$

nodes.name: Eichler-Shimura congruence identifies $N_\ell(n)$ with point counts
nodes.statement: By Eichler-Shimura congruence, $N_{\ell}(n)=|\widetilde{X}(\F_{\ell^n})|$.
assumptions: For a prime $\ell\neq p$, the curve $X=X_0^+(p^2)$ has good reduction at $\ell$
conclusions: $N_{\ell}(n)=|\widetilde{X}(\F_{\ell^n})|$

nodes.name: The cumulative point count $R_\ell(n)$
nodes.statement: $R_{\ell}(n):=|\cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{ s\,i}})|$

nodes.name: The parity sequence $P_\ell(n)$
nodes.statement: the sequence of integers $\{ P_\ell(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ defined by $$0\leq P_\ell (n)\leq 1\,\,\text{ and }\,\, P_{\ell}(n)=R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)\pmod 2\,,$$
nodes.statement_short: $P_\ell(n)\in\{0,1\}$ records the parity of the increment $R_\ell(n+1)-R_\ell(n)$.

nodes.name: Inclusion-exclusion recursion for $R_\ell(n+1)-R_\ell(n)$
nodes.statement: More precisely, if $\{p_1,\cdots,p_r\}$ is the set of primes dividing $n+1$ and we put $d_i=(n+1)/p_i$ for $1\leq i\leq r$, then $$ R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)= P_\ell (s(n+1))-\sum_ {j=1}^r (-1)^{r-1} \sum_{1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_j\leq r} P_\ell (s \gcd(d_{i_1},\cdots,d_{i_j}))\,.$$
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion-exclusion over the prime divisors of $n+1$ expresses the increment of $R_\ell$ through the $P_\ell$ values.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (elimination of $p\in\{17,19,23,29,31\}$)
nodes.statement: Assume that, for $p\in\{17,19,23,29,31\}$, there is a nontrivial automorphism $u\in\Aut_K(X_0^+(p^2))$. By Lemma \ref{invo}, we can suppose that $u$ is an involution. Let $g_u$ be the genus of the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/u$. We know that $u$ has at most $12$ fixed points. By Riemann-Hurwitz formula, we get that the number of fixed points by $u$ must be even, say $2r$, and, moreover, $$ g_u=\frac{g^++1-r}{2}\,,\quad 0\leq r\leq 6\,. $$ If $g^+$ is even, then $u$ can have $2$, $6$ or $10$ ramification points, while for the case $g^+$ odd, $u$ can have $0$, $4$, $8$ or $12$ such points. For a prime $\ell\neq p$, the curve $X=X_0^+(p^2)$ has good reduction at $\ell$. Let $\widetilde{X}$ be the reduction of $X$ modulo $\ell$. We write $$ N_{\ell}(n):=1+\ell^n-\sum_{i=1}^{2 g^+}\alpha_i^n\,, $$ where $\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_{2 g^+}$ are the roots of polynomial $$ \prod_{f\in \New_{p^2}^+\cup\New_p}(x^2-a_{\ell}(f) x+\ell) $$ and $a_{\ell}(f)$ is the $\ell$-th Fourier coefficient of $f$. By Eichler-Shimura congruence, $N_{\ell}(n)=|\widetilde{X}(\F_{\ell^n})|$. Let $\gl$ be a prime of $K$ over $\ell$ with residue degree $s$. The reduction of $X\otimes K$ modulo $\gl$ is $\widetilde X\otimes \F_{\ell^s}$ which has an involution, say $\widetilde u$, with at most $2r$ fixed points. The automorphism $\widetilde u$ acts on the set $\widetilde{X}(\F_{\ell^{s\, n}})$ as a permutation. If $Q\in \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$, then the set $\cS_Q=\{ \widetilde{u}^i(Q)\colon 1\leq i \leq 2\}$ is contained in $ \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$ and its cardinality is equal to $1$ or $2$ according to $Q$ is a fixed point of $\widetilde u$ or not. Hence, almost all integers $R_{\ell}(n):=|\cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{ s\,i}})|$, $n\geq 1$, are equivalent to the number of fixed points of $\widetilde{u}$ mod $2$ and, moreover, the sequence $\{R_\ell (n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ changes of parity depending on whether $N_{\ell}(s)$ is even or odd. In other words, the sequence of integers $\{ P_\ell(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ defined by $$0\leq P_\ell (n)\leq 1\,\,\text{ and }\,\, P_{\ell}(n)=R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)\pmod 2\,,$$ can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ ones according to $N_{\ell^s}$ being even or odd. Note that the integer $R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)$ can be obtained from the sequence $\{ N_\ell (s\, n)\}$ by using $$\widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cap \widetilde X(\F_{\ell ^{s\, d_2}})=\widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,\gcd(d_1,d_2)}})\,,\quad\text{ and if } d_1|d_2 \text{ then }\widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cup \widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,d_2}})=\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{s\,d_2}})\,. $$ More precisely, if $\{p_1,\cdots,p_r\}$ is the set of primes dividing $n+1$ and we put $d_i=(n+1)/p_i$ for $1\leq i\leq r$, then $$ R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)= P_\ell (s(n+1))-\sum_ {j=1}^r (-1)^{r-1} \sum_{1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_j\leq r} P_\ell (s \gcd(d_{i_1},\cdots,d_{i_j}))\,.$$ For the five possibilities for $p$, we have: \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=31$:} $g^+=30$, $2r\leq 10$ and $\ell=2$ splits in $K=\Q(\sqrt{-31})$. One has $$ N_2(1)=9\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 36}P_2(n)=10\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm {$p=29$:} $g^+=26$, $2r\leq 10$ and $\ell=2$ is inert in $K=\Q(\sqrt{29})$. One has $$ N_2(2)=42\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 42}P_2(n)=11\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=23$:} $g^+=15$, $2r\leq 12$ and $\ell=2$ splits in $K=\Q(\sqrt{-23})$. One has $$ N_2(1)=8\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 38}P_2(n)=13\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=19$:} $g^+=9$, $2r\leq 12$ and $\ell=2$ is inert in $K=\Q(\sqrt{-19})$. One has $$N_2(2)=22\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 46 } P_2(n)=13\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=17$:} $g^+=7$, $2r\leq 12$ and $\ell=2$ splits in $K=\Q(\sqrt{17})$. One has $$ N_2(1)=6\,,\quad\quad\sum_{n\leq 46}P_2(n)=13\,. $$ So, we can discard the five cases considered and the statement is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce mod $2$ and count parity changes of $|\widetilde X(\F_{2^{sn}})|$: the observed number of parity changes exceeds the Riemann-Hurwitz bound $2r$ for each of the five primes, so no nontrivial automorphism exists.

nodes.name: Reduce to an involution with at most $12$ fixed points
nodes.statement: Assume that, for $p\in\{17,19,23,29,31\}$, there is a nontrivial automorphism $u\in\Aut_K(X_0^+(p^2))$. By Lemma \ref{invo}, we can suppose that $u$ is an involution. Let $g_u$ be the genus of the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/u$. We know that $u$ has at most $12$ fixed points.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the contradiction hypothesis and reduce to an involution with at most $12$ fixed points.

nodes.statement: By Riemann-Hurwitz formula, we get that the number of fixed points by $u$ must be even, say $2r$, and, moreover, $$ g_u=\frac{g^++1-r}{2}\,,\quad 0\leq r\leq 6\,. $$ If $g^+$ is even, then $u$ can have $2$, $6$ or $10$ ramification points, while for the case $g^+$ odd, $u$ can have $0$, $4$, $8$ or $12$ such points.

nodes.name: Point counts of the reduction via Eichler-Shimura
nodes.statement: For a prime $\ell\neq p$, the curve $X=X_0^+(p^2)$ has good reduction at $\ell$. Let $\widetilde{X}$ be the reduction of $X$ modulo $\ell$. nodes.statement_short: Introduce $N_\ell(n)$ from the Fourier coefficients and identify it with $|\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^n})|$.

nodes.name: Parity-change bound from the induced involution
nodes.statement: Let $\gl$ be a prime of $K$ over $\ell$ with residue degree $s$. The reduction of $X\otimes K$ modulo $\gl$ is $\widetilde X\otimes \F_{\ell^s}$ which has an involution, say $\widetilde u$, with at most $2r$ fixed points. The automorphism $\widetilde u$ acts on the set $\widetilde{X}(\F_{\ell^{s\, n}})$ as a permutation. If $Q\in \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$, then the set $\cS_Q=\{ \widetilde{u}^i(Q)\colon 1\leq i \leq 2\}$ is contained in $ \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$ and its cardinality is equal to $1$ or $2$ according to $Q$ is a fixed point of $\widetilde u$ or not. Hence, almost all integers $R_{\ell}(n):=|\cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{ s\,i}})|$, $n\geq 1$, are equivalent to the number of fixed points of $\widetilde{u}$ mod $2$ and, moreover, the sequence $\{R_\ell (n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ changes of parity depending on whether $N_{\ell}(s)$ is even or odd. In other words, the sequence of integers $\{ P_\ell(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ defined by $$0\leq P_\ell (n)\leq 1\,\,\text{ and }\,\, P_{\ell}(n)=R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)\pmod 2\,,$$ can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ ones according to $N_{\ell^s}$ being even or odd.

nodes.name: Computing the increments by inclusion-exclusion
nodes.statement: Note that the integer $R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)$ can be obtained from the sequence $\{ N_\ell (s\, n)\}$ by using $$\widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cap \widetilde X(\F_{\ell ^{s\, d_2}})=\widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,\gcd(d_1,d_2)}})\,,\quad\text{ and if } d_1|d_2 \text{ then }\widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cup \widetilde X (\F_{\ell ^{s\,d_2}})=\widetilde X(\F_{\ell^{s\,d_2}})\,. $$ More precisely, if $\{p_1,\cdots,p_r\}$ is the set of primes dividing $n+1$ and we put $d_i=(n+1)/p_i$ for $1\leq i\leq r$, then $$ R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)= P_\ell (s(n+1))-\sum_ {j=1}^r (-1)^{r-1} \sum_{1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_j\leq r} P_\ell (s \gcd(d_{i_1},\cdots,d_{i_j}))\,.$$
nodes.statement_short: Express the increments of $R_\ell$ effectively from the $N_\ell(sn)$ by inclusion-exclusion over subfields.
